results.summary: This design implements a digital binary FSK modem for underwater acoustic communication in the 46-56 kHz band, using 48 kHz for mark and 54 kHz for space. It transmits and receives framed data with preamble, sync word, payload, and CRC-8, generating samples via a numerically controlled oscillator and decoding with parallel Goertzel filters. The chip interfaces through SPI for configuration and data transfer, and provides several debug outputs for monitoring. Notable limitations include half-duplex operation and lack of symbol-timing recovery, which may require multiple frames for initial synchronization.

TeenyTPU is a 2x2 INT8 systolic array TPU that performs matrix multiplication, producing 16-bit partial sums. It is controlled via an SPI slave interface with opcodes for loading weights and activations, starting computation, and reading results. The design includes a control FSM and status flags (busy, done) for synchronization. It requires an external SPI master for configuration and data transfer, and is intended for accelerating neural network or DSP workloads.

This design is a multicycle CPU that executes programs written in the BF (Brainfuck) language. It has no on-chip RAM; both program and data tape reside in an external SPI RAM emulated by an RP2040 running spi-ram-emu. The CPU uses an on-chip SPI master to access memory, performing at least one SPI transaction per instruction. It is tested with cocotb and requires an external RP2040 for memory, making it suitable for educational purposes.

This is a GNSS accelerator that implements acquisition and tracking for GPS L1 signals, including Gold code generation, NCO for frequency correction, and early/mid/late tracking. It interfaces with a MAX2769 or MAX2771 front-end via SPI for configuration and receives quantized I/Q samples. The design provides SPI slave registers for control and readback, and an interrupt output for frame timing or acquisition events. It requires a custom hardware setup with a GNSS front-end and an RP2040 for software interaction, and testing may be limited due to hardware availability.

This design is a minimal RV32E microcontroller SoC with a UART program loader, internal instruction memory, GPIO, and configurable 7-segment output. It can boot from internal memory or load a program via UART, and it supports a demo program that drives seven-segment displays. The core includes 16 registers and supports a subset of RISC-V instructions. It requires an external USB-UART adapter for loading programs and can drive a 7-segment display directly.

This is a controller for an 8-sensor line-following robot car. It reads digital signals from an IR sensor array, computes a tracking error using a weighted method, and generates PWM signals for two DC motors to correct the trajectory. Four configuration pins allow tuning of the correction magnitude for more aggressive or smoother turns. The design requires external hardware including an 8-channel IR sensor array, analog comparators, dual DC motors, an H-bridge driver, and configuration switches.

This project is a VGA screensaver that displays a bouncing logo with the text UACJ and A.M.G on a 640x480 @ 60 Hz screen. It is based on a DVD screensaver design and includes modules for VGA sync generation and bitmap ROM. The logo moves around the screen and changes color upon hitting edges. It requires a VGA display and a VGA PMOD or breakout board with a resistor DAC for connection.

This design implements a small two-layer neural network with 4 hidden neurons that predicts digits 0-9 from 7-segment display patterns. It takes the 7 segment inputs and outputs a 4-bit prediction. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and no details on training, accuracy, or testing. It likely requires no external hardware beyond input switches and output LEDs for verification.

This is a simple Pong game with VGA-style output, supporting two players and an auto mode. The documentation is essentially a work-in-progress placeholder with no details on how it works or how to test it. It likely requires a VGA display and buttons for player input, but this is inferred from the pin names. The design is not sufficiently documented to provide a complete summary.

This is a digital PWM generator with selectable resolution (5-9 bits), dyadic modulation, and dithering modes. It produces complementary high-side and low-side outputs with dead-time, plus a sync clock. The design is configured via a register file written over the pins, and it defaults to 8-bit normal PWM after reset. It is intended for power electronics applications such as buck converters or class-D stages, and requires no external hardware for bench testing.
